reference.source: Mann's Surgery of the Foot and Ankle
clinicalPearls: Hallux rigidus is osteoarthritis of the first metatarsophalangeal joint, characterised by pain and progressive loss of dorsiflexion of the great toe
A dorsal osteophyte on the metatarsal head produces a palpable dorsal bump and causes dorsal impingement pain at the extremes of extension
Pain is typically worst at toe-off during walking and when wearing heeled or stiff-toed shoes that force dorsiflexion
In earlier disease (hallux limitus) motion is limited but the joint is relatively preserved, whereas advanced disease shows global cartilage loss and marked stiffness
Grind and dorsal impingement tests reproduce pain, and the range of dorsiflexion should be compared with the unaffected side
Weight-bearing radiographs demonstrate joint-space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis, dorsal osteophytes, and periarticular cysts
Conservative management uses a stiff-soled or rocker-bottom shoe, a rigid insole to limit painful motion, activity modification, and intra-articular corticosteroid injection
Surgical choices depend on disease stage and include dorsal cheilectomy for early impingement and arthrodesis for advanced arthritis, with arthroplasty in selected patients
reference.pathophysiology: Hallux rigidus is degenerative arthritis of the first metatarsophalangeal joint in which cartilage wear begins dorsally on the metatarsal head, where compressive and shear loads concentrate during dorsiflexion at push-off. Reactive bone forms a dorsal osteophyte on the metatarsal head and often the proximal phalanx, which mechanically blocks dorsiflexion and impinges painfully at the extremes of extension. Over time the wear becomes global with joint-space narrowing, subchondral sclerosis and cyst formation, and the toe becomes progressively stiff. Contributing factors include previous trauma or osteochondral injury, an elevated or long first metatarsal, inflammatory or crystal arthropathy, and possibly a familial predisposition. As dorsiflexion is lost the patient rolls onto the outer border of the foot at toe-off, which can produce lateral forefoot overload and secondary symptoms.
additionalDifferentials: Hallux valgus with a painful medial eminence
Gout or pseudogout of the first metatarsophalangeal joint
Turf toe or other capsuloligamentous injury of the first metatarsophalangeal joint
Inflammatory arthritis such as rheumatoid or psoriatic disease
Septic arthritis of the first metatarsophalangeal joint
Osteochondral lesion of the metatarsal head
additionalInvestigations: Weight-bearing dorsoplantar and lateral foot radiographs to grade joint-space narrowing and dorsal osteophytes
Clinical measurement of dorsiflexion and plantarflexion compared with the contralateral toe
Dorsal impingement and axial grind tests to localise pain to the joint
Serum urate and inflammatory markers where crystal or inflammatory disease is suspected
Joint aspiration and microscopy if acute inflammation or infection cannot be excluded clinically
MRI in selected cases to assess an osteochondral lesion or early cartilage change
Response to a diagnostic intra-articular local anaesthetic injection to confirm the pain source
redFlags: Acutely hot, red, swollen joint suggesting gout, pseudogout, or septic arthritis rather than degenerative disease
Systemic features or polyarticular involvement indicating inflammatory arthropathy
Rest pain, night pain, or a destructive appearance on imaging out of keeping with simple osteoarthritis
Ulceration or infection over the dorsal bump, particularly in diabetes or vascular disease
reference.prognosis: Symptoms usually progress slowly with fluctuating pain and increasing stiffness. Many patients are controlled long term with footwear and insole modification and occasional injections. Cheilectomy relieves dorsal impingement well in early to moderate disease, and arthrodesis is a reliable and durable procedure for advanced arthritis that reliably relieves pain at the cost of joint motion. Progression of arthritis after motion-preserving surgery is possible.
pitfalls: Mistaking a painful dorsal osteophyte for a hallux valgus bunion and directing treatment to the wrong deformity
Performing cheilectomy alone in advanced global arthritis, which fails because the whole joint surface is worn
Missing acute gout or infection presenting as a suddenly painful, swollen first metatarsophalangeal joint
Neglecting footwear and insole modification before considering surgery
Overlooking lateral forefoot overload that develops as the patient offloads the stiff great toe
references: Mann's Surgery of the Foot and Ankle
management: Footwear modification with a stiff-soled or rocker-bottom shoe and a Morton's extension orthosis to limit painful first metatarsophalangeal dorsiflexion
Activity modification and NSAIDs for symptomatic relief
Intra-articular corticosteroid injection for painful flares
Cheilectomy to remove the dorsal osteophyte and relieve impingement in early to moderate disease
First metatarsophalangeal arthrodesis as a durable option for advanced global degeneration
Joint-preserving arthroplasty or implant in selected patients as an alternative to fusion
Escalate to surgical referral when footwear, orthoses and injections fail to control symptoms
